name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q01 - Order of reactivity of alcohols with halogen acids

questiontext.text:
The order of reactivity of following alcohols with halogen acids is

(A) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)

(B) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH(CH_3)-OH}\)

(C) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-OH}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alcohols react with halogen acids (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) via a nucleophilic substitution reaction in which protonation of the hydroxyl group is followed by cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond to form a carbocation intermediate. The rate of reaction depends on the stability of the carbocation formed.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structures
Propan-1-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH_2-OH}\), is a primary (\(1^\circ\)) alcohol that forms a primary carbocation. Butan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH(CH_3)-OH}\), is a secondary (\(2^\circ\)) alcohol that forms a secondary carbocation. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-OH}\), is a tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) alcohol that forms a tertiary carbocation.

Step 3: Application of Carbocation Stability
Due to the \(+I\) inductive effect of alkyl groups and hyperconjugation, carbocation stability follows the order \(3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ\). Consequently, the reactivity of alcohols towards halogen acids decreases in the order \(3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The reactivity order from most reactive to least reactive is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-OH} > \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH(CH_3)-OH} > \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH_2-OH}\), which corresponds to \(\mathrm{(C) > (B) > (A)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q02 - Alcohol yielding alkyl chloride with concentrated HCl

questiontext.text: Which of the following alcohols will yield the corresponding alkyl chloride on reaction with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) at room temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Lucas test (reaction of alcohols with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\)), tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) alcohols react rapidly at room temperature without requiring a catalyst (\(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\)) because they form a highly stable tertiary carbocation intermediate.

Step 2: Evaluation of Alcohols
Propan-1-ol (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)) and 2-methylbutan-1-ol (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2OH}\)) are primary (\(1^\circ\)) alcohols, while butan-2-ol (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-CH(CH_3)-OH}\)) is a secondary (\(2^\circ\)) alcohol; these require anhydrous \(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\) or heating to react at an appreciable rate. In contrast, 2-methylbutan-2-ol (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-OH}\)) is a tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) alcohol.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the tertiary alcohol \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-OH}\) yields the corresponding alkyl chloride on reaction with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) at room temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q03 - Identify compound Y in Sandmeyer reaction

questiontext.text: Identify the compound \(\mathrm{Y}\) in the following reaction.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary aromatic amines undergo diazotisation when treated with nitrous acid (generated in situ from \(\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}\)) at \(273\text{--}278\text{ K}\) to form arenediazonium salts. Subsequent treatment with cuprous chloride (\(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}\)) replaces the diazonium group with a chlorine atom via the Sandmeyer reaction.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Reaction
Aniline (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)) reacts with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}\) at \(273\text{--}278\text{ K}\) to form benzenediazonium chloride (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\)). Upon treatment with \(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}\), nitrogen gas (\(\mathrm{N_2}\)) is evolved and a single chlorine atom is introduced onto the benzene ring.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The compound \(\mathrm{Y}\) formed in this reaction is chlorobenzene (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q04 - Reaction of toluene with halogen and FeCl3

questiontext.text: Toluene reacts with a halogen in the presence of iron (III) chloride giving ortho and para halo compounds. The reaction is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aromatic rings are electron-rich \(\pi\)-systems and characteristically undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as \(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\).

Step 2: Application to Toluene
Iron (III) chloride (\(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\)) acts as a Lewis acid and polarises the halogen molecule (\(\mathrm{X_2}\)) to generate a halonium electrophile (\(\mathrm{X^+}\)). This electrophile attacks the aromatic ring of toluene, substituting a hydrogen atom at the ortho and para positions (because the \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) group is ortho- and para-directing).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the reaction is an electrophilic substitution reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q05 - Identification of halogen exchange reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following is halogen exchange reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A halogen exchange reaction is one in which a halogen atom in an alkyl halide is replaced by another halogen atom. A classic example is the Finkelstein reaction, where an alkyl chloride or bromide reacts with sodium iodide (\(\mathrm{NaI}\)) in dry acetone to form an alkyl iodide.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reactions
The reaction \(\mathrm{RX + NaI \longrightarrow RI + NaX}\) directly exchanges the halide \(\mathrm{X^-}\) with \(\mathrm{I^-}\). In contrast, addition of \(\mathrm{HX}\) across an alkene is an electrophilic addition reaction, reaction of \(\mathrm{R-OH}\) with \(\mathrm{HX}\) in the presence of \(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\) substitutes a hydroxyl group rather than a halogen, and reaction of toluene with \(\mathrm{X_2}\) in the presence of \(\mathrm{Fe}\) in the dark is an electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{RX + NaI \longrightarrow RI + NaX}\) is the halogen exchange reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q06 - Reagent for free radical chlorination of butane

questiontext.text:
Which reagent will you use for the following reaction?

\[\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3 \longrightarrow CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl + CH_3CH_2CHClCH_3}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkanes undergo substitution of hydrogen atoms by chlorine via a free radical mechanism when treated with chlorine gas in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light or heat.

Step 2: Application to Butane
In n-butane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3}\)), UV light homolytically cleaves \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) into chlorine free radicals (\(\mathrm{Cl^\bullet}\)), which abstract primary and secondary hydrogens to produce a mixture of 1-chlorobutane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl}\)) and 2-chlorobutane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHClCH_3}\)). Other reagents such as \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) in the dark or \(\mathrm{NaCl + H_2SO_4}\) do not initiate free radical chlorination of alkanes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The required reagent is \(\mathrm{Cl_2 / UV\text{ light}}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gas in the presence of iron in dark

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q07 - Increasing order of densities of haloarenes

questiontext.text: Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their densities.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For structurally similar aromatic compounds and haloarenes, density increases with an increase in the number of halogen atoms and the atomic mass of the halogen substituent, because molecular mass increases substantially while molecular volume changes comparatively little.

Step 2: Evaluation of Compounds
Benzene, (a), has no halogen atom and has the lowest molecular mass. Chlorobenzene, (b), has one chlorine atom (atomic mass \(35.5\text{ u}\)). 1,3-Dichlorobenzene, (c), has two chlorine atoms. 1-Bromo-3-chlorobenzene, (d), has one chlorine atom and one heavier bromine atom (atomic mass \(80\text{ u}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the density increases with increasing molecular mass in the order \(\mathrm{(a) < (b) < (c) < (d)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q08 - Increasing order of boiling points of bromobutanes

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their boiling points.

(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)-CH_2Br}\)

(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\)

(c) \(\mathrm{H_3C-C(CH_3)(Br)-CH_3}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For isomeric alkyl halides with the same molecular formula, boiling point depends on intermolecular van der Waals forces, which are proportional to the surface area of the molecule. As branching increases, the molecule becomes more compact and spherical, reducing its surface area and lowering its boiling point.

Step 2: Evaluation of Isomers
Compound (b), 1-bromobutane, is an unbranched straight-chain isomer with the largest surface area and therefore the highest boiling point. Compound (a), 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, has one branch and an intermediate surface area. Compound (c), 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, is the most highly branched isomer, giving it the smallest surface area and the lowest boiling point.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of boiling points is \(\mathrm{(c) < (a) < (b)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q09 - Identifying asymmetric carbon atoms in molecules

questiontext.text:
In which of the following molecules carbon atom marked with asterisk (\(*\)) is asymmetric?

(a)   (b)   (c)   (d)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom is an \(sp^3\)-hybridised carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Molecule
In molecule (a), the marked carbon is bonded to four different atoms: \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{I}\), \(-\mathrm{Br}\), and \(-\mathrm{Cl}\). In molecule (b), the marked carbon is bonded to four different atoms: \(-\mathrm{D}\), \(-\mathrm{I}\), \(-\mathrm{Br}\), and \(-\mathrm{Cl}\). In molecule (c), the marked carbon is bonded to four different groups/atoms: \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{OH}\), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\), and \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\). In molecule (d), however, the marked carbon is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms (\(-\mathrm{H}\)) along with \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), so it is not asymmetric.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The carbon atom marked with an asterisk is asymmetric in molecules \(\mathrm{(a), (b), (c)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q10 - Identifying enantiomeric structure of 2-bromobutane

questiontext.text:
Which of the following structures is enantiomeric with the molecule (A) given below:

(A)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other, meaning they have opposite absolute configurations (\(R\) versus \(S\)) at the chiral centre. Interchanging any two groups at a chiral centre inverts its configuration, producing its enantiomer.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structures
In molecule (A), the chiral carbon is bonded to \(-\mathrm{H}\) (up, in-plane), \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) (down-left, in-plane), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) (dash, away), and \(-\mathrm{Br}\) (wedge, towards). Using Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules (\(-\mathrm{Br} > -\mathrm{C_2H_5} > -\mathrm{CH_3} > -\mathrm{H}\)), molecule (A) has the \(R\)-configuration. The structure with \(-\mathrm{H}\) (up, in-plane), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) (down-left, in-plane), \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) (dash, away), and \(-\mathrm{Br}\) (wedge, towards) is obtained by swapping the \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) and \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups of (A), which gives the opposite \(S\)-configuration. The remaining three structures represent the same \(R\)-configuration as (A) viewed from different orientations.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the structure with \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) in-plane and \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) on the dash (with \(-\mathrm{H}\) up and \(-\mathrm{Br}\) on the wedge) is the enantiomer of molecule (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q11 - Example of vicinal dihalide

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of vic-dihalide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vicinal dihalides (vic-dihalides) are dihaloalkanes in which two halogen atoms are attached to two adjacent carbon atoms in the carbon chain.

Step 2: Evaluation of Compounds
Dichloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}\)) has both chlorine atoms on the same carbon atom, making it a geminal dihalide. Ethylidene chloride (\(\mathrm{CH_3CHCl_2}\)) also has both chlorine atoms on the same carbon atom (geminal dihalide). Allyl chloride (\(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_2Cl}\)) contains only one chlorine atom and is a monohalide. 1,2-Dichloroethane (\(\mathrm{ClCH_2-CH_2Cl}\)) has two chlorine atoms attached to adjacent carbons (\(\mathrm{C1}\) and \(\mathrm{C2}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, 1,2-dichloroethane is an example of a vic-dihalide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q12 - Classification of bromine position in allylic compound

questiontext.text: The position of \(-\mathrm{Br}\) in the compound in \(\mathrm{CH_3CH=CHC(Br)(CH_3)_2}\) can be classified as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An allylic halide is a compound in which the halogen atom is bonded to an \(sp^3\)-hybridised carbon atom that is directly adjacent to a carbon–carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{C=C}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Structure
In \(\mathrm{CH_3CH=CHC(Br)(CH_3)_2}\), the carbon bearing the \(-\mathrm{Br}\) group is \(sp^3\)-hybridised and is directly attached to the \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon of the \(\mathrm{CH=CH}\) double bond. Moreover, this carbon is attached to three other carbon atoms, making it a tertiary carbon rather than a secondary, vinylic, or aryl carbon.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the position of \(-\mathrm{Br}\) is classified as allyl.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q13 - Electrophilic species in chlorination of benzene

questiontext.text: Chlorobenzene is formed by reaction of chlorine with benzene in the presence of \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\). Which of the following species attacks the benzene ring in this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogenation of benzene in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) proceeds via electrophilic aromatic substitution.

Step 2: Mechanism of Electrophile Generation
The Lewis acid \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) coordinates with \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) to polarise the \(\mathrm{Cl-Cl}\) bond, generating the chloronium ion (\(\mathrm{Cl^+}\)) and the tetrachloroaluminate ion (\([\mathrm{AlCl_4}]^-\)): \(\mathrm{Cl_2 + AlCl_3 \longrightarrow Cl^+ + [AlCl_4]^-}\). The electron-rich benzene ring then attacks the electrophile \(\mathrm{Cl^+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The species that attacks the benzene ring in this reaction is \(\mathrm{Cl^+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q14 - Classification of ethylidene chloride

questiontext.text: Ethylidene chloride is a/an

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dihaloalkanes having both halogen atoms attached to the same carbon atom are called geminal dihalides (gem-dihalides) and are commonly named as alkylidene halides.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structure
The chemical formula of ethylidene chloride is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHCl_2}\) (1,1-dichloroethane). Both chlorine atoms are bonded to the same terminal carbon atom.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, ethylidene chloride is a gem-dihalide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q15 - Addition of HCl to allylbenzene

questiontext.text: What is ‘A’ in the following reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrophilic addition of hydrogen halides (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) to an unsymmetrical alkene follows Markovnikov’s rule: the proton (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) adds to the double-bonded carbon atom with more hydrogen atoms so as to generate the more stable carbocation intermediate, which is then attacked by the halide ion (\(\mathrm{Cl^-}\)).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
In allylbenzene (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\)), protonation occurs at the terminal \(=\mathrm{CH_2}\) carbon (which has two hydrogens) to form the more stable secondary carbocation \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3}\) rather than the primary carbocation \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H_2}\). Nucleophilic attack by \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) on the secondary carbocation gives \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-CH(Cl)-CH_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, product ‘A’ is 2-chloro-1-phenylpropane (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-CH(Cl)-CH_3}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q16 - Preferred nucleophilic substitution for primary alkyl halide

questiontext.text: A primary alkyl halide would prefer to undergo

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) proceeds via a concerted backside attack by the nucleophile and is favoured by low steric hindrance at the reactive carbon. Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) proceeds through a carbocation intermediate and is favoured by stable (\(3^\circ\) or resonance-stabilised) carbocations.

Step 2: Application to Primary Alkyl Halides
A primary alkyl halide (\(\mathrm{R-CH_2-X}\)) has minimal steric crowding around the \(\alpha\)-carbon, allowing easy backside attack by a nucleophile. Furthermore, a primary carbocation is highly unstable, which prevents the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) pathway (and racemisation).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, a primary alkyl halide prefers to undergo an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q17 - Reactivity of tert-butyl halides in SN1 reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following alkyl halides will undergo \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction most readily?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The rate-determining step of an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction is the heterolytic cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond to form a carbocation and a halide ion. When the alkyl group is identical, the rate depends on the leaving-group ability of the halogen and the strength of the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond.

Step 2: Comparison of Carbon–Halogen Bonds
Among the halides \(\mathrm{F, Cl, Br, I}\), atomic size increases down the group, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond length increases and bond dissociation enthalpy decreases in the order \(\mathrm{C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I}\). Consequently, the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond breaks most easily, and \(\mathrm{I^-}\) is the best leaving group.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-I}\) undergoes the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction most readily.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q18 - IUPAC name of 1-bromo-2-methylbutane

questiontext.text: Which is the correct IUPAC name for \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(C_2H_5)-CH_2-Br}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to IUPAC nomenclature rules, select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent alkane, number it to give the substituents the lowest possible locants, and list substituents in alphabetical order.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Naming
Expanding \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\) as \(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH_3}\), the longest continuous carbon chain contains four carbon atoms (butane): \(\mathrm{Br-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3}\). Numbering from the end nearer to the bromine atom gives \(\mathrm{C1}\) for \(-\mathrm{Br}\) and \(\mathrm{C2}\) for \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\). Listing substituents alphabetically places bromo before methyl.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct IUPAC name is 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q19 - IUPAC name for diethylbromomethane

questiontext.text: What should be the correct IUPAC name for diethylbromomethane?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To convert a common name into an IUPAC name, write out the full structural formula, identify the longest continuous carbon chain, and number it to assign the lowest locant to the substituent.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Naming
Diethylbromomethane consists of a central \(\mathrm{-CH(Br)-}\) group attached to two ethyl (\(\mathrm{-CH_2CH_3}\)) groups: \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(Br)-CH_2-CH_3}\). The longest continuous carbon chain has five carbon atoms (pentane), with the bromo substituent located at position 3 from either end.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct IUPAC name is 3-Bromopentane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q20 - Chlorination of toluene in presence of iron in dark

questiontext.text: The reaction of toluene with chlorine in the presence of iron and in the absence of light yields

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as iron (which forms \(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\) in situ) and in the absence of light, arenes undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution rather than side-chain free radical halogenation.

Step 2: Directive Influence of the Methyl Group
The methyl group (\(-\mathrm{CH_3}\)) on toluene is electron-releasing by inductive (\(+I\)) and hyperconjugation effects, making it an ortho- and para-directing group. Consequently, the chloronium electrophile (\(\mathrm{Cl^+}\)) attacks predominantly at the ortho (C2) and para (C4) positions of the benzene ring.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The reaction yields a mixture of o-chlorotoluene (2-chlorotoluene) and p-chlorotoluene (4-chlorotoluene).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q21 - Ammonolysis of chloromethane with excess ammonia

questiontext.text: Chloromethane on treatment with excess of ammonia yields mainly

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution with ammonia (ammonolysis) to form amines. When the alkyl halide is in excess, further alkylation yields secondary amines, tertiary amines, and quaternary ammonium salts. However, when a large excess of ammonia is used, the primary amine is obtained as the major product.

Step 2: Application to Chloromethane
Chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\)) reacts with excess \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) via \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow CH_3NH_2 + NH_4Cl}\). Because ammonia is present in large excess, the probability of \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\) reacting with \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\) to form secondary or tertiary amines is minimised.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the main product formed is methanamine (\(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\)).

answer.text: Mixture containing all these in equal proportion

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q22 - Identifying a chiral molecule

questiontext.text: Molecules whose mirror image is non superimposable over them are known as chiral. Which of the following molecules is chiral in nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A molecule with a single tetrahedral carbon atom is chiral if that carbon is bonded to four different atoms or groups (an asymmetric or chiral carbon), resulting in a non-superimposable mirror image.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structures
1-Bromobutane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\)) has no carbon with four different groups. 2-Bromopropane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_3}\)) has two identical \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups on \(\mathrm{C2}\). 2-Bromopropan-2-ol (\(\mathrm{CH_3C(Br)(OH)CH_3}\)) also has two identical \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups on \(\mathrm{C2}\). In 2-bromobutane (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(Br)-CH_2CH_3}\)), \(\mathrm{C2}\) is bonded to four different groups: \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{Br}\), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\), and \(-\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, 2-Bromobutane is chiral in nature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q23 - Mechanism of benzyl bromide with aqueous NaOH

questiontext.text: Reaction of \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br}\) with aqueous sodium hydroxide follows

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) is strongly favoured when the substrate can dissociate to form a highly stable carbocation intermediate, especially in a polar protic solvent such as water.

Step 2: Stability of the Carbocation Intermediate
Although benzyl bromide (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br}\)) is a primary halide, heterolytic cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond produces the benzyl carbocation (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2^+}\)). This carbocation is extensively stabilised by resonance with the aromatic benzene ring, making its stability comparable to that of a secondary or tertiary carbocation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the reaction of \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br}\) with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) follows the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism.

answer.text: Any of the above two depending upon the temperature of reaction

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q24 - Asymmetric carbon atoms in 2,3-dihydroxy-4-oxobutanoic acid

questiontext.text: Which of the carbon atoms present in the molecule given below are asymmetric?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom must be \(sp^3\)-hybridised and bonded to four different atoms or groups.

Step 2: Evaluation of Labelled Carbons
Carbon \(a\) (in \(-\mathrm{COOH}\)) and carbon \(d\) (in \(-\mathrm{CHO}\)) are \(sp^2\)-hybridised and doubly bonded to oxygen, so they cannot be asymmetric. Carbon \(b\) is \(sp^3\)-hybridised and bonded to four different groups: \(-\mathrm{COOH}\), \(-\mathrm{OH}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), and \(-\mathrm{CH(OH)CHO}\). Similarly, carbon \(c\) is \(sp^3\)-hybridised and bonded to four different groups: \(-\mathrm{CHO}\), \(-\mathrm{OH}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), and \(-\mathrm{CH(OH)COOH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, only carbons \(b\) and \(c\) are asymmetric.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q25 - Formation of racemic mixture on nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text:
Which of the following compounds will give racemic mixture on nucleophilic substitution by \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) ion?

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A racemic mixture (an equimolar mixture of \(d\)- and \(l\)-enantiomers) is formed upon nucleophilic substitution when the leaving group is attached directly to a chiral carbon and the reaction proceeds through a planar carbocation intermediate (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism), allowing \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) to attack from either face.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structures
In compound (a), 2-bromobutane, the \(-\mathrm{Br}\) atom is directly attached to a chiral carbon bonded to \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), and \(-\mathrm{Br}\); substitution via a planar carbocation yields both enantiomers of butan-2-ol (a racemic mixture). In compound (b), 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, the carbon bearing \(-\mathrm{Br}\) has two identical \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups, so the product is achiral. In compound (c), 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, the \(-\mathrm{Br}\) is attached to a primary achiral carbon (\(-\mathrm{CH_2Br}\)); substitution does not break any bond to the adjacent chiral carbon, so no racemisation occurs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only compound \(\mathrm{(a)}\) gives a racemic mixture on nucleophilic substitution by \(\mathrm{OH^-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q26 - Rate of nucleophilic substitution in nitrochlorobenzenes

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution.

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_NAr}\)) in haloarenes proceeds via a negatively charged Meisenheimer complex intermediate. Electron-withdrawing groups such as \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) increase the reaction rate by stabilising this negative charge, especially when located at the ortho or para positions where resonance stabilisation occurs.

Step 2: Comparison of Compounds
Chlorobenzene, (a), has no electron-withdrawing group and is the least reactive. 1-Chloro-3-nitrobenzene, (c), has a \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) group at the meta position, which stabilises the intermediate only through the inductive (\(-I\)) effect without resonance delocalisation onto the nitro group. 1-Chloro-2-nitrobenzene, (b), has a \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) group at the ortho position, which strongly stabilises the carbanion intermediate by both \(-R\) (resonance) and \(-I\) effects.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of rate towards nucleophilic substitution is \(\mathrm{(a) < (c) < (b)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q27 - Rate of nucleophilic substitution with multiple nitro groups

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution.

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The rate of nucleophilic aromatic substitution in aryl halides increases with the number of electron-withdrawing \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) groups present at the ortho and para positions relative to the halogen atom, because they disperse the negative charge of the Meisenheimer intermediate by resonance.

Step 2: Comparison of Compounds
Chlorobenzene, (a), has no \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) group and reacts the slowest. 1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene, (b), has one \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) group at the para position, giving an intermediate rate. 2-Chloro-1,3,5-trinitrobenzene, (c), has three \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) groups (two ortho and one para), providing maximum stabilisation of the intermediate and the fastest rate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of rate towards nucleophilic substitution is \(\mathrm{(a) < (b) < (c)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q28 - Effect of methyl groups on nucleophilic substitution of chlorobenzene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution.

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron-releasing groups such as \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) at the ortho and para positions increase electron density on the benzene ring and destabilise the negatively charged intermediate formed during nucleophilic aromatic substitution, thereby decreasing the reaction rate.

Step 2: Comparison of Compounds
1-Chloro-2,4-dimethylbenzene, (c), has two electron-releasing \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups (at ortho and para positions), causing the greatest destabilisation and the lowest reactivity. 4-Chlorotoluene, (b), has one \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) group at the para position, giving intermediate reactivity. Chlorobenzene, (a), has no electron-releasing group and therefore reacts fastest among the three.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of rate towards nucleophilic substitution is \(\mathrm{(c) < (b) < (a)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q29 - Rate of nucleophilic substitution in chlorotoluenes

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution.

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron-donating \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups retard nucleophilic aromatic substitution by destabilising the carbanion intermediate. This destabilisation is much stronger when the \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) group is ortho or para to the leaving group (via both \(+I\) effect and hyperconjugation, plus steric hindrance at the ortho position) than when it is meta.

Step 2: Comparison of Compounds
In 2-chlorotoluene, (a), the ortho \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) group exerts both strong electronic destabilisation and steric hindrance near the reaction centre, making it the least reactive. In 3-chlorotoluene, (b), the meta \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) group exerts only a weak \(+I\) effect. Chlorobenzene, (c), lacks any electron-donating substituent and is the most reactive of the three.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of rate towards nucleophilic substitution is \(\mathrm{(a) < (b) < (c)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q30 - Increasing order of boiling points of 1-halobutanes and butane

questiontext.text:
Which is the correct increasing order of boiling points of the following compounds?

1-Iodobutane, 1-Bromobutane, 1-Chlorobutane, Butane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For compounds with the same alkyl chain, boiling point increases with molecular mass and the size/polarisability of the halogen atom because stronger van der Waals dispersion forces and dipole–dipole interactions exist between larger, more polarisable molecules.

Step 2: Comparison of Compounds
Butane is a non-polar alkane with the lowest molecular mass and weakest intermolecular forces, giving it the lowest boiling point. Among the 1-halobutanes, atomic mass and polarisability increase in the order \(\mathrm{Cl < Br < I}\), so the boiling points increase from 1-chlorobutane to 1-bromobutane to 1-iodobutane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of boiling points is \(\text{Butane} < \text{1-Chlorobutane} < \text{1-Bromobutane} < \text{1-Iodobutane}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q31 - Increasing order of boiling points of bromoalkanes and bromobenzene

questiontext.text:
Which is the correct increasing order of boiling points of the following compounds?

1-Bromoethane, 1-Bromopropane, 1-Bromobutane, Bromobenzene

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For compounds containing the same halogen atom, boiling point increases with increasing molecular mass and surface area because larger molecules experience stronger intermolecular van der Waals forces of attraction.

Step 2: Comparison of Compounds
The molecular masses and carbon chain sizes increase from 1-bromoethane (\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br}\), \(109\text{ u}\)) to 1-bromopropane (\(\mathrm{C_3H_7Br}\), \(123\text{ u}\)) to 1-bromobutane (\(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\), \(137\text{ u}\)) to bromobenzene (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br}\), \(157\text{ u}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of boiling points is \(\text{1-Bromoethane} < \text{1-Bromopropane} < \text{1-Bromobutane} < \text{Bromobenzene}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q85 - Phosphorus chlorides vs thionyl chloride

questiontext.text:
Assertion: Phosphorus chlorides (tri and penta) are preferred over thionyl chloride for the preparation of alkyl chlorides from alcohols.

Reason: Phosphorus chlorides give pure alkyl halides.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Thionyl chloride (\(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\)) is preferred over phosphorus chlorides (\(\mathrm{PCl_3}\) or \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\)) for preparing alkyl chlorides from alcohols because the byproducts of the thionyl chloride reaction (\(\mathrm{SO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\)) are gases that escape, leaving behind pure alkyl chloride. Hence, the assertion is wrong.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
Reactions of alcohols with \(\mathrm{PCl_3}\) or \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) produce non-volatile byproducts such as \(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\) or \(\mathrm{POCl_3}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\), which require separation from the alkyl chloride. Therefore, phosphorus chlorides do not directly yield pure alkyl halides, and the reason is also wrong.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are wrong statements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q86 - Boiling points of alkyl halides

questiontext.text:
Assertion: The boiling points of alkyl halides decrease in the order: \(\mathrm{RI > RBr > RCl > RF}\)

Reason: The boiling points of alkyl chlorides, bromides and iodides are considerably higher than that of the hydrocarbon of comparable molecular mass.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
For the same alkyl group (\(\mathrm{R}\)), the size and atomic mass of the halogen increase from \(\mathrm{F}\) to \(\mathrm{I}\). Larger halogen atoms have greater polarisability and stronger van der Waals dispersion forces, so boiling points decrease in the order \(\mathrm{RI > RBr > RCl > RF}\). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
Alkyl halides have greater polarity and higher molecular mass than hydrocarbons of comparable size, leading to stronger dipole–dipole and van der Waals attractions, and hence higher boiling points. Thus, the reason is also a correct statement, but it compares haloalkanes to hydrocarbons rather than explaining the trend among \(\mathrm{RI, RBr, RCl, RF}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q87 - Reaction of KCN with methyl chloride

questiontext.text:
Assertion: \(\mathrm{KCN}\) reacts with methyl chloride to give methyl isocyanide

Reason: \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) is an ambient nucleophile.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Potassium cyanide (\(\mathrm{KCN}\)) is predominantly ionic in nature and provides free \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) ions in solution. Attack occurs mainly through the carbon atom because the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond is stronger than the \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bond, yielding methyl cyanide (\(\mathrm{CH_3CN}\)) as the major product rather than methyl isocyanide. Hence, the assertion is wrong.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
The cyanide ion (\(\mathrm{CN^-}\)) is an ambident nucleophile because it can donate an electron pair through either its carbon atom (forming cyanides/nitriles) or its nitrogen atom (forming isocyanides). Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is wrong, but the reason is a correct statement.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q88 - Wurtz reaction of tert-butyl bromide

questiontext.text:
Assertion: tert-Butyl bromide undergoes Wurtz reaction to give 2, 2, 3, 3-tetramethylbutane.

Reason: In Wurtz reaction, alkyl halides react with sodium in dry ether to give hydrocarbon containing double the number of carbon atoms present in the halide.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Tertiary alkyl halides such as tert-butyl bromide are sterically hindered and undergo elimination (dehydrohalogenation) rather than coupling in the presence of sodium in dry ether, forming isobutylene and isobutane instead of 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane. Hence, the assertion is wrong.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
In the Wurtz reaction, alkyl halides (typically primary) react with metallic sodium in dry ether to yield a symmetrical alkane containing double the number of carbon atoms present in the alkyl halide. Thus, the reason is a correct statement.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is wrong, but the reason is a correct statement.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q89 - Effect of nitro group on nucleophilic substitution of haloarenes

questiontext.text:
Assertion: Presence of a nitro group at ortho or para position increases the reactivity of haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution.

Reason: Nitro group, being an electron withdrawing group decreases the electron density over the benzene ring.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Haloarenes are normally unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution, but introducing a nitro (\(-\mathrm{NO_2}\)) group at the ortho or para position markedly increases their reactivity. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason and Connection
The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing (\(-R\) and \(-I\)), which decreases the electron density on the benzene ring and stabilises the negatively charged Meisenheimer complex intermediate formed during nucleophilic attack. This directly explains the increased reactivity of ortho- and para-nitrohaloarenes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q90 - Electrophilic substitution in monohaloarenes

questiontext.text:
Assertion: In monohaloarenes, further electrophilic substitution occurs at ortho and para positions.

Reason: Halogen atom is a ring deactivator.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
In monohaloarenes, the lone pairs on the halogen atom participate in resonance (\(+R\) effect) with the benzene ring, increasing electron density at the ortho and para positions. Consequently, further electrophilic substitution occurs predominantly at the ortho and para positions. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
Because halogens are strongly electronegative, their inductive (\(-I\)) electron-withdrawing effect outweighs the resonance (\(+R\)) effect, reducing overall electron density on the ring and making the halogen atom a ring deactivator. Thus, the reason is also correct, but it explains the lower reactivity rather than the ortho/para orientation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q91 - Preparation of aryl iodides using oxidising agent

questiontext.text:
Assertion: Aryl iodides can be prepared by reaction of arenes with iodine in the presence of an oxidising agent.

Reason: Oxidising agent oxidises \(\mathrm{I_2}\) into \(\mathrm{HI}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Direct iodination of arenes is reversible because the byproduct \(\mathrm{HI}\) reduces the aryl iodide back to the arene. Carrying out the reaction in the presence of an oxidising agent such as \(\mathrm{HIO_3}\) or \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) drives the reaction forward to yield aryl iodides. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
The role of the oxidising agent is to oxidise the \(\mathrm{HI}\) formed during the reaction back into \(\mathrm{I_2}\), not to oxidise \(\mathrm{I_2}\) into \(\mathrm{HI}\). Therefore, the reason is wrong.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, but the reason is a wrong statement.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q92 - Reactivity of C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene vs chloroethane

questiontext.text:
Assertion: It is difficult to replace chlorine by \(-\mathrm{OH}\) in chlorobenzene in comparison to that in chloroethane.

Reason: Chlorine-carbon (\(\mathrm{C-Cl}\)) bond in chlorobenzene has a partial double bond character due to resonance.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Nucleophilic substitution of \(-\mathrm{Cl}\) by \(-\mathrm{OH}\) in chlorobenzene requires drastic conditions (such as \(623\text{ K}\) and \(300\text{ atm}\)), whereas chloroethane undergoes hydrolysis readily under mild conditions. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason and Connection
In chlorobenzene, the lone pair on the chlorine atom conjugates with the \(\pi\)-electrons of the benzene ring, giving the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond partial double bond character. This makes the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond shorter and stronger than the pure single \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond in chloroethane, directly explaining why it is much harder to cleave.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q93 - Stereochemistry of hydrolysis of (-)-2-bromooctane

questiontext.text:
Assertion: Hydrolysis of (\(-\))-2-bromooctane proceeds with inversion of configuration.

Reason: This reaction proceeds through the formation of a carbocation.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
Hydrolysis of optically active (\(-\))-2-bromooctane with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) proceeds via an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism, in which the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving bromide group, resulting in complete inversion of configuration. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
An \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction is a concerted single-step process that passes through a pentacoordinate transition state without forming any carbocation intermediate (carbocation formation occurs in \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reactions and leads to racemisation). Thus, the reason is wrong.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, but the reason is a wrong statement.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANESANDHALOARENES_MCQ_Q94 - Nitration of chlorobenzene

questiontext.text:
Assertion: Nitration of chlorobenzene leads to the formation of m-nitrochlorobenzene

Reason: \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) group is a m-directing group.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Assertion
In chlorobenzene, the chlorine substituent is ortho- and para-directing due to its \(+R\) resonance effect. Therefore, nitration of chlorobenzene yields a mixture of o-nitrochlorobenzene and p-nitrochlorobenzene, not m-nitrochlorobenzene. Hence, the assertion is wrong.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reason
The nitro group (\(-\mathrm{NO_2}\)) is a strongly electron-withdrawing group that withdraws electron density particularly from the ortho and para positions of a benzene ring, making it a meta-directing group for further electrophilic substitution. Thus, the reason is a correct statement.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is wrong, but the reason is a correct statement.
